ImageDescription.value: This species ranges in size from 3–18 centimetres (1.2–7.1 in) and is a burrower, constructing U-shaped holes in the loose substrate near the bases of coral reefs in water ranging from 3–40 metres (9.8–131.2 ft). It's a smasher, with club-shaped raptorial appendages. An agile and active intertidal and sub-intertidal predator, it prefers gastropods, crustaceans, and bivalves, and will repeatedly deliver blunt force to the exoskeleton of its prey until it can gain access to the underlying soft tissue for consumption. It is reported to have a "punch" of over 80 km/h (50 miles/h), the fastest recorded punch of any living animal. The acceleration is similar to that in a .22 LR bullet fired from a handgun.

ImageDescription.value:
A water flea of genus Daphnia photographed under a microscope using an 8x objective. The specimen was collected on August 7, 2023, from a pond in the city of Rakvere, Estonia. The lateral view excellently demonstrates the transparent carapace of the water flea, allowing observation of its internal structure. Particularly striking are the orange embryo in the dorsal brood pouch and the greenish digestive tract filled with food particles. Daphnia are among the most common planktonic organisms in freshwater and play a crucial role in aquatic food webs.
The specimen was photographed against a black background, which emphasizes the structures of the transparent shell. The lighting technique used was reflected light from a photographic speedlight flash, which particularly highlights the surface patterns and internal anatomy. The image was created using focus stacking technique, which ensures great depth of field throughout the subject.

ImageDescription.value:
A male water mite (Arrenurus sp.) photographed under a microscope using an 8x objective. The specimen was collected in June 2023. The image clearly shows the characteristic pear-shaped body form of male water mites and their distinctive posterior extension, which is the main feature distinguishing males from females. The body surface displays a characteristic reticulated pattern and red eyes. The appendages are transparent and covered with spiny bristles.
The specimen was photographed against a black background, which creates a strong contrast with the yellowish-brown body surface texture and fine details of the appendages. The lighting technique used was reflected light from a photographic speedlight flash, which particularly emphasizes the surface structures and patterns. The image was created using focus stacking technique, which ensures great depth of field throughout the subject.

ImageDescription.value:
A water flea of genus Daphnia photographed under a microscope using an 8x objective. The specimen was collected on July 9, 2023. Of particular interest is the dark resting egg or ephippium in the dorsal brood pouch - this is a specialized resistant structure that forms when environmental conditions become unfavorable. The production of resting eggs is a survival strategy of water fleas, allowing them to survive adverse conditions, similar to plant seeds. The transparent body also shows a characteristic reticulated pattern and bluish tints.
The specimen was photographed against a black background, which highlights the transparent carapace and the dark resting egg within. The lighting technique used was reflected light from a photographic speedlight flash, which particularly emphasizes the surface structures. The image was created using focus stacking technique, which ensures great depth of field throughout the subject.

ImageDescription.value: A water mite (Hydrachnidia) photographed under a microscope using an 8x objective. The specimen was collected in June 2023. Water mites show considerable variation in color and body patterns between species - this specimen displays characteristic white patches on its brownish body. The image clearly shows the typical spherical body in lateral view and appendages covered with setae. A dark region of internal organs is visible through the semi-transparent carapace. The image was captured using reflected light, which particularly emphasizes the surface structure and fine details of the appendages. The image was created using focus stacking technique, which ensures great depth of field throughout the subject.

Categories.value: Cataclysta lemnata|Self-published work|Featured pictures of animals in Estonia|Focus stacking images of Lepidoptera|Featured pictures by Janek Lass

ImageDescription.value: The image depicts the larva of Cataclysta lemnata, an aquatic species that lives entirely underwater and constructs protective cases from plants using silk. The larvae primarily consume the invasive duckweed Lemna minuta, a plant known for its rapid growth and negative impacts on ecosystems. C. lemnata is a multivoltine species, with several generations per year, allowing its larvae to feed continuously throughout the year. In later developmental stages, the larvae consume large amounts of plant material, making them effective biocontrol agents. The larvae also use Lemna plants not only for food but to construct floating cases, which protect them from predators and aid buoyancy. This species is a remarkable example of adaptation to aquatic life, as the larvae breathe dissolved oxygen directly through their thin skin. This specimen is about 15-20mm long.
